extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, patent litigators, jury instruction drafters, and patent attorneys involved in U.S. design-patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for evaluating validity, enforceability, priority, and damages in U.S. design patent litigation. Covers obviousness, anticipation/priority, inequitable conduct, written description/enablement/indefiniteness, inventorship, double patenting, and damages rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice and diligence (priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interruptions necessitated by the everyday problems and obligations of the inventor or others working with him or her do not prevent a finding of diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining priority under 35 U.S.C. §102(g), consider respective dates of conception and reduction to practice and the reasonable diligence of one who was first to conceive and last to reduce to practice, from a time prior to conception by the other. Design inventions are reduced to practice as soon as an embodiment is constructed; ornamental design may be reduced to practice upon filing unless prior construction is shown. (Cited authorities: Hupp; Continental Plastic Containers; Mas v. Root.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention was known or used by others in this country, or patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country, before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic anticipation analysis: a single prior art reference that discloses the claimed invention can invalidate. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §102(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation/Prior US applications or patents (35 U.S.C. §102(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention was described in an application for patent, published under section 122(b), by another filed in the United States before the invention by the applicant for patent, or a patent granted on an application filed in the United States before the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes U.S. filed/issued patents or published U.S. applications filed prior to the applicant's invention; special rules apply to international applications (designation, publication in English).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation (35 U.S.C. §102(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant did not himself invent the subject matter sought to be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges based on someone else being the true inventor (derivation) are governed by §102(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention by another (35 U.S.C. §102(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: During an interference or in priority disputes, another inventor may establish that before the person's invention the invention was made by such other inventor and not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority under §102(g) considers conception, reduction to practice, and reasonable diligence; the court must consider whether the other inventor made the invention first in the U.S. and did not abandon/suppress/conceal it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness – general (design patent §103 analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed design is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill who designs articles of the type involved; determine if combining a primary and a closely related secondary reference would suggest the claimed design to such a designer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a designer of ordinary skill would have combined the references to create the same overall visual appearance. Primary references must teach a specific design (not a design concept) and look basically the same as the claimed design. Obviousness may be shown by more than one item of prior art, but references must be so related that ornamental features in one would suggest application to the other. The defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. (Factors enumerated below should be evaluated.) (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §103; In re Rosen; Durling; In re Cho; KSR.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness – required factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Five factors that must be evaluated to determine obviousness of a design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) The scope and content of the prior art relied upon; 2) The differences, if any, between the claimed design and the prior art; 3) The level of ordinary skill in the art at the time the design was made; 4) Whether the ordinary observer would find the two designs substantially the same; 5) Additional considerations indicating obviousness or not. Each factor must be evaluated (in any order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness – differences with the prior art (analysis of differences and analogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed design from the view of a designer of ordinary skill, determining the impact of such differences on obviousness of the design as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of relevant prior art extends to all 'analogous arts' (surface-appearance designs consider any prior art with similar surface appearance; form designs limit analogous art to similar types of articles). Do not require precise appearance in prior art; consider inferences and creative steps a designer would have employed. Combining known elements in a known fashion is generally not patentable; however, a new material element can create a new integral design. Showing each element was independently known is insufficient—consider whether a reason/motivation existed at the time to combine elements (prior art, background knowledge, problem to solve, market demand, common sense). Prior art that 'teaches away' may support non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designer of ordinary skill in the art (definition and identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness determination is based on the perspective of the ordinary designer skilled in the art, presumed familiar with relevant prior art designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ordinary designer is not any designer but one who designs articles of the type involved. Parties may agree to an identity for that person; if not agreed, the jury should consider what attributes define such an ordinary designer. (Cited: Titan Tire; Durling; In re Carter; In re Borden.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness – secondary (objective) indicia of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain factors, if established, may indicate the design was not obvious; no single factor is dispositive and the design must be considered as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only appropriate instructions. Examples of secondary considerations: (1) commercial success due to appearance rather than advertising or other features; (2) long-felt need for a new look; (3) others tried but failed to create the design; (4) others copied the claimed design; (5) unexpectedly superior appearance over closest prior art; (6) praise or admiration from others or defendant; (7) licensing acceptance because of the appearance. Answering yes to any of these may suggest nonobviousness. (Cited: Graham factors; Sash Controls; Avia Group.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity – lack of ornamentality (functionality doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents protect ornamental appearance; if the overall appearance is dictated solely by how it works, the patent is invalid because the design is not 'ornamental.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is normal that designs perform some function; the question is whether the general functional characteristics can only be embodied by the claimed design or whether alternate designs perform substantially the same function. Existence of alternate designs may be strong evidence that the design was not dictated solely by function. A design need not be aesthetically pleasing; lack of artistic merit does not disqualify patentability. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §171; Best Lock; Seiko Epson; Hupp.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unenforceability – inequitable conduct (duty of candor and good faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant has a duty to prosecute patent applications with candor, good faith, and honesty; intentional failure to meet that duty is inequitable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty extends to all inventors named, patent attorneys/agents involved in prosecution, and every other person substantially involved. Defendant must prove inequitable conduct by clear and convincing evidence. Courts may choose various ways to present the issue (jury or court) and may break out materiality, intent, and balancing in verdict forms. (Cited: AIPLA Model; Flex-Rest.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct – materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Material information is information a reasonable examiner would be substantially likely to consider important in deciding whether to allow the application to issue as a patent; materiality is not limited to prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material information is non-cumulative and either: (1) establishes, by itself or with other information, a prima facie case of unpatentability of a claim; or (2) refutes or is inconsistent with positions the applicant has taken (opposing PTO arguments or asserting patentability). Information that is cumulative or adds little to what examiner had is not material. Note: PTO standard changed Jan 17, 1992 (effective Mar 16, 1992); Federal Circuit has applied both pre- and post-1992 standards in cases. (Cited: 37 C.F.R. §1.56(b); Digital Control; Cargill; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct – intent to deceive or mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: If material information was withheld/misrepresented/submitted falsely, determine whether that was done with intent to deceive or mislead the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct evidence of intent is rare; intent may be inferred from facts and surrounding circumstances. When a patentee knowingly misrepresents a material fact or submits false material information and the natural consequence would be to deceive the PTO, an inference of intent may be appropriate. Simple negligence is insufficient. Consider the totality of circumstances including nature of conduct and evidence of good faith. (Cited: AIPLA Model; Cargill; eSpeed; Purdue Pharma; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct – balancing materiality and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: If materiality and intent are proven by clear and convincing evidence, balance their degrees to determine whether inequitable conduct occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where withheld/misrepresented information is highly material, less proof of intent to deceive is needed; conversely, high proof of intent may require less materiality. The court/jury must weigh both to reach a clear and convincing showing of inequitable conduct. (Cited: eSpeed; Cargill; Purdue Pharma; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity – written description requirement for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent must contain a written description and drawing of the design claimed; insufficient description/drawings render the patent invalid if they fail to enable understanding of what the claimed design looks like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that errors, variations, or inconsistencies between drawings or written description are consequential. Design patent written description is evaluated with regard to whether a designer of ordinary skill can understand the claimed design from the specification/drawings. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §112; related cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity – enablement (design patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description must contain enough detail to teach or enable persons skilled in the art to understand how the design looks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents are written for designers of ordinary skill; they need not expressly show information that such a designer would be likely to know or could obtain. Written description is enabling so long as undue experimentation is not required; permissible experimentation is appropriate to the complexity of the design field and the expertise of persons skilled in that field. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §112; Seed Lighting decision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity – indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The design patent claim (drawings and written description) must be sufficiently clear that a designer of ordinary skill can determine what the design looks like; otherwise the claim is indefinite and invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amount of detail required depends on particular design, prior art, and the description. Drawings read with the description must reasonably inform a designer of ordinary skill. Lack of absolute precision is not automatically indefinite; there is a presumption of validity and deference to the examiner who issued the patent. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §112 ¶2; In re Zahn; DCNL v. Almar Sales.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity – improper inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent invalidity can be asserted for improper inventorship if the patent does not name all actual inventors and only the actual inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be an inventor, one must make a significant contribution to the claimed design, measured against the scope of the claimed design. Persons may be joint inventors even if they did not physically work together, but must have some open line of communication during or near the time of their inventive effort. Explaining known concepts, suggesting ideas or design concepts, or merely carrying out another's instructions (helping with experimentation) does not make someone an inventor. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §§116, 256; Eli Lilly; Slip Track; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity – double patenting (design vs utility two-way test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent may be invalid for double patenting over a utility patent or application where the features producing the novel aesthetic effect of the design are the same as those recited in the claims of a utility patent as producing a novel structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a two-way test: (a) whether the subject matter of the design-claim would have been obvious from the subject matter of the utility claim(s); and (b) whether the subject matter of the utility claim(s) would have been obvious from the design claim. If the two-way test is satisfied, the design patent is invalid as obvious over the utility patent or application. (Cited: In re Dembiczak; Shelcore; Carman; In re Thorington.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages – general (measure of recovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement and validity are found, the plaintiff may elect compensatory damages (actual damages) or may elect to recover the defendant's profits as a measure of recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instructions guide calculation of damages if the jury finds infringement and that the design patent is not invalid. The plaintiff indicates which measure (compensatory damages or defendant's profits) it seeks to prove. (Cited: 35 U.S.C. §§284, 289; Catalina Lighting.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages – commencement of damages and marking/notice rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Date from which damages or defendant's profits begin depends on whether the patent was granted before the infringing activity and on notice/marking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patent granted before infringing activity began, calculate damages/profits from date infringement began. If patent granted after infringing activity began, calculate from the patent-issue date (or agreed date). If marking is at issue, recovery is limited to acts after the plaintiff gave notice (actual or constructive). Actual notice is communication of a specific charge of infringement and is effective as of the date given. Service of a complaint alleging patent infringement normally effects notice. The parties may agree on a commencement date; if so, instruct accordingly.
